artifactEvidence.excerpt: Zimperium says the malware then tries to persuade the person to turn on Accessibility access. That setting can let an app read what is on screen and interact with apps on a person’s behalf. Accessibility is also used by legitimate disability tools, so the useful question is which app is asking, why it needs that access and whether you trust its developer.

An app file downloaded from a link is not the same as an app installed from Google Play. Play Protect is Google’s built-in app safety check: Google says it scans apps from Play and other sources and can warn, disable or remove potentially harmful apps. Keep it on.

Restricted settings are Android’s extra pause for sensitive access from an app installed outside Google Play. Google says not to allow them unless you trust the developer. A real accessibility app may need access to read a screen or help someone interact with it; that is why this is a review step, not a reason to switch accessibility off everywhere.

explainBack.question: Why can't RatHat infect an Android phone from a text message alone, and why does it still want Accessibility access once installed?
explainBack.answer: According to the article, the text or ad only carries a link to a deceptive download page; the person must manually download and install the app file outside the Play Store, so the message itself does nothing without that human step. Once installed, the malware persuades the person to enable Accessibility because that setting lets an app read whatever is on screen and act inside other apps on the person's behalf — which is exactly the control a credential-stealing app needs, and why legitimate disability tools also use it.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer must cite the manual-download step outside Play as the required link in the chain (P002) and Accessibility's screen-reading/app-interaction capability plus its legitimate uses (P003).
explainBack.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this answer in ordinary language; both causal links are explicit in P002 and P003, so explain-back passes.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A reader's parent gets a WhatsApp message claiming their bank's app is 'expiring' with a link to download an 'updated' version. After installing it, the app displays a screen saying 'Enable Accessibility to keep your account secure.'
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's model, what should the parent do at each step, and why?
unseenTransfer.answer: At the link step: the download bypasses Google Play, which is the article's first checkpoint — stop and instead open Google Play or the bank's official website to get the real app (P006). If already installed: the Accessibility request is the second checkpoint — a bank app has no legitimate need to read the whole screen and act in other apps, so the parent should refuse, check the developer, and let Play Protect scan and remove it if flagged (P004, P005). The 'security' framing is exactly the localized lure the report describes.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Correct application of the two-checkpoint model — install source and sensitive-access justification — plus the developer-trust test and Play Protect fallback from P004–P006.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism resolves this novel scenario cleanly at both checkpoints, so unseen transfer passes.
